doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: John Hammond and integration of the Goodman band
summary: He knew John Hammond and tells how Hammond got Goodman to hire Teddy Wilson in 1935, and about earlier hidden integrated jamming.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: No. That’s what I talk about in my class and that’s where integration — when John Hammond, who I’m sure you know, knew, or know of — well I was lucky enough to know John Hammond. He worked at two labels, Columbia and Vanguard. I worked at two labels, Columbia and Vanguard. And I got to know Mr. Hammond in the 80s. He died in ’87. But he was the guy who integrated the Goodman band in 1935 by getting him to hire Teddy Wilson and then Lionel Hampton and then Charlie Christian. And he told me stories that are just scary, the stuff he ran into. Then he signed Count Basie, then he signed Billie Holiday and on and on, then in the 60s Bob Dylan, Bruce Springsteen.

Well he signed Aretha to Columbia but it was not successful. Columbia took her over and tried to make her into a pop singer. It wasn’t ‘til she went to Atlantic. But he told me all those stories, and what a guy. But I talk about it in my class, in 1935 when he convinced Benny Goodman to hire Teddy Wilson, which I said would be equivalent to, I don’t know, whoever’s out there now, Hammond sending a man from Mars. It was front page. Not entertainment section, it was front page. “Goodman Breaks the Color Barrier.” I’ve got the headlines on film and stuff. But that was twelve years before Jackie Robinson went into the major leagues. It was music that integrated first. Now before that, black and white musicians were getting together up in Harlem and playing at night at these joints Mel Powell and them told me about. They just couldn’t tell anybody. They couldn’t tell the sponsors, or people about it. Otherwise they’d be blackballed.
Plus they were playing together on recordings, right?
It wasn’t ‘til Hammond that they played integrated sessions.

I’ve got pictures Mr. Hammond gave me of John Hammond leading a section. It was Benny Goodman; Freddie Green, Basie’s guitarist; Basie playing piano; Buck Clayton playing trumpet. It was an integrated band. But Goodman, John Hammond told me, Goodman couldn’t let other people know about that. Otherwise the band would be banned for integrating, behind the scenes. They played up in Harlem at nights, and places in LA. They were jamming. Especially in Harlem. But it was in ’35 when Hammond convinced Benny to hire Teddy Wilson, that they integrated. And that became headline news. Yup. It was music who integrated society. And like you say, the white kids, all they cared about was we love this music. Back then, and when I was playing a lot, in the 60s and when it was white kids going to those dances. They weren’t integrated dances for the most part. They were white audiences or we’d play in black clubs with black artists and black audiences.
